Naked
NAY-kid
adj.
Old English nacod, bare, unclothed. Webster 1828: not covered; bare; having no clothes on; also, open to view, manifest, unarmed, destitute. In the Authorized Version naked is the condition sin produced in Eden and the condition every man will be in before God unless he is clothed by Another.

Biblical Definition

Naked is the Bible’s word for exposure, and it enters Scripture at the fall. Before sin the man and his wife were naked and not ashamed; after it, the eyes of them both were opened, and they knew that they were naked; and they sewed fig leaves together, and made themselves aprons (Genesis 3:7). Nakedness itself did not change — their standing did. The first human industry was the manufacture of a covering, and God replaced it with coats of skins, which required a death. From there the word carries the whole doctrine. Job strips the question to its frame: Naked came I out of my mother's womb, and naked shall I return thither (Job 1:21). Nothing is carried in and nothing out. Hebrews applies it to the reader now rather than later: all things are naked and opened unto the eyes of him with whom we have to do (Hebrews 4:13). And the risen Christ diagnoses a wealthy congregation with the word they would least expect — thou art wretched, and miserable, and poor, and blind, and naked (Revelation 3:17) — and offers white raiment to buy from Him. The pattern never varies: man notices his nakedness, man sews something, God provides the covering. Fig leaves are the whole history of self-righteousness in one verse.

Webster 1828 Definition

Webster 1828 defines NAKED as not covered; bare; having no clothes on; open to view, not concealed, manifest; unarmed, defenceless; destitute of means of defence or support; also, plain, evident, undisguised.

expand to see more

NAKED, a. [Sax. nacod.] — Not covered; bare; having no clothes on. Unarmed; defenceless; open; exposed; subject to. Open to view; not concealed; manifest. Destitute of means of defence or support. Plain; evident; undisguised; as the naked truth.

Every one of Webster’s senses is used somewhere in Scripture, and they converge on Hebrews 4:13 — all things are naked and opened unto the eyes of him. There the word is simultaneously uncovered, defenceless, manifest, and undisguised. The English idiom the naked truth is the same figure, and it is the reason the word can name both the sinner’s shame and God’s sight of it.

Key Scripture

Genesis 3:7 — "And the eyes of them both were opened, and they knew that they were naked; and they sewed fig leaves together, and made themselves aprons."

Job 1:21 — "And said, Naked came I out of my mother's womb, and naked shall I return thither: the LORD gave, and the LORD hath taken away; blessed be the name of the LORD."

Hebrews 4:13 — "Neither is there any creature that is not manifest in his sight: but all things are naked and opened unto the eyes of him with whom we have to do."

Revelation 3:17 — "Because thou sayest, I am rich, and increased with goods, and have need of nothing; and knowest not that thou art wretched, and miserable, and poor, and blind, and naked:"

Revelation 16:15 — "Behold, I come as a thief. Blessed is he that watcheth, and keepeth his garments, lest he walk naked, and they see his shame."

Modern Corruption

Naked is corrupted when the shame that entered at the fall is treated as the real problem — a false modesty to be unlearned — rather than as the true signal of a real guilt, so that the remedy becomes self-acceptance instead of a covering God provides.

expand to see more

A now-standard account reads Genesis 3 as the origin of an unhealthy shame about the body, and prescribes the removal of the shame. Scripture prescribes the removal of the guilt. Adam and Eve were naked before the fall and unashamed; the body did not change, the standing did. Their shame was accurate — it was the conscience reporting a real breach — and God did not correct the diagnosis. He accepted it and answered it, replacing the fig leaves with coats of skins, which required the death of an animal and taught in one act that acceptable covering is provided, substitutionary, and costly. Any counsel that treats the shame as the disease leaves the guilt untouched and the man still uncovered, and it must ignore what God actually did in the garden.

The second corruption is the church’s own, and Revelation 3 names it. A congregation may be prosperous, active, and entirely satisfied — I am rich, and increased with goods, and have need of nothing — and be described by Christ as naked. Self-assessment is not the instrument by which spiritual condition is measured, which is why Hebrews 4:13 puts the reader under a gaze rather than in front of a mirror. The Laodicean remedy is instructive: they are counselled to buy white raiment of Him. Not to work on their self-perception, and not to sew. The only covering Scripture recognizes is the imputed righteousness of Christ, received by faith, and the fig leaf is what men make when they would rather manufacture a covering than receive one.

Greek & Hebrew Roots

The Hebrew and Greek words for naked are plain and physical, and Scripture’s theology comes from where it places them — at the fall, at the grave, and before the throne. The Greek of Hebrews 4:13 adds a second image the English keeps: laid bare, with the neck exposed.

expand to see more

Hebrew ārōm — naked, bare (Genesis 3:7; Job 1:21). Untagged in this lexicon; no Strong’s page is minted for it here.

Greek gumnos — naked, unclothed, poorly clad (Hebrews 4:13; Revelation 3:17; Revelation 16:15). The root of English gymnasium. Untagged in this lexicon.

Hebrew bōsh — to be ashamed, to be confounded; the companion word from Genesis 2:25 onward, joining nakedness to shame from the start. Untagged in this lexicon.

The second word in Hebrews 4:13, rendered opened, carries the sense of a neck bent back and exposed — the posture of a sacrifice under the knife.

Usage

"They knew that they were naked and sewed fig leaves (Genesis 3:7) — the first human industry was the manufacture of a covering."

"Naked came I out of my mother's womb (Job 1:21): nothing is carried in, and nothing out."

"Laodicea was rich and naked at the same time (Revelation 3:17); self-assessment does not measure the soul’s condition."
